rationale: Clinical authorities and consensus diagnostic descriptions (such as GeneReviews and reviews by Verstraeten & Dietz) maintain that ectopia lentis is not a feature of Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS) and serves as a primary discriminator distinguishing LDS from Marfan syndrome. However, aggregated cohort and systematic review data (such as Loomba et al., 2022) identify documented ectopia lentis in 2 out of 275 LDS patients. The available literature does not provide definitive slit-lamp re-evaluations proving that these specific documented instances were misattributions or phenocopies (such as microspherophakia or high myopia) rather than true lens subluxation, creating a direct conflict between clinical diagnostic dogma and aggregated empirical reports.

evidence.text: In a comprehensive review of ocular manifestations across Loeys-Dietz syndrome cohorts, documented ectopia lentis was identified in a small minority of patients (2 out of 275), demonstrating that the finding is occasionally recorded in LDS literature despite standard diagnostic exclusion criteria.

conflicts: GeneReviews and core clinical references state that ectopia lentis is never observed in Loeys-Dietz syndrome and serves as an exclusion criterion, whereas systematic aggregation of LDS cohorts reports documented ectopia lentis in 2/275 individuals.

The literature currently lacks granular slit-lamp or genetic re-evaluations confirming whether the 2 reported cases were diagnostic misclassifications, phenocopies (such as microspherophakia), dual pathology (e.g., co-occurring FBN1 variant), or true secondary zonular failure.

new_directions.question_text: Do patients in multi-gene aortopathy registries with SMAD2 mutations and reported ectopia lentis carry unrecognized secondary variants in FBN1, ADAMTS10, or LTBP2?
new_directions.rationale: Testing for dual molecular diagnoses in reported atypical cases would resolve whether ectopia lentis can be genuinely driven by perturbed TGF-beta signaling or represents co-inherited fibrillinopathy.
